newsitem.title: MEXICO: Foreign banks invade Mexican retail market.
newsitem.headline: Foreign banks invade Mexican retail market.

text.p: Foreign banks are making an unexpectedly powerful foray into Mexican retail banking, shaking up an industry that once looked to outsiders only as lenders.

The invasion into commercial banking is almost exclusively from Spain -- causing left-wing Mexican congressmen to refer to it as the "reconquest" -- and it has occured with a speed and scope that has made even top-tier Mexican banks edgy.

"A lot of Mexican banks have begun to get worried, especially banks like Banamex and Bancomer that are very strong in this sector," said Rogelio Urrutia, banking analyst at Mexican brokerage Valores Finamex.

With flashy advertisements, a string of new products and new branches across Mexico, Spain's Banco Bilbao Vizcaya has led the charge, buying up and renaming what was previously Grupo Financiero Mercantil Probursa, and taking over the outlets of smaller groups Banca Cremi and Banorie.

Bital, in which Spain's Banco Credito Hispano and Portugal's Banco Comercial Portugues have minority stakes, has also set up clusters of small branches, innovatively opened on Saturdays and extended week-day business into the early evening.
Banco Santander of Spain brought Grupo Financiero Invermexico in October, and is already advertising as if it will bring major changes to its subsidiary's image and name in the near future.
"We're now seeing that retail banking is also being strongly attacked by foreigners," said Laura Berdeja, director of Latin American financial analysis at Santander Investment.

"It had been anticipated that foreign banks would focus exclusively on competing in the corporate area, but that's not what has happened," she added, explaining that hopes of a recovery in domestic consumption were spurring the drive.

The timing for foreign banks could not have been better. Mexico began to crack open its closed financial system during negotiations for the North American Free Trade Agreement with the United States and Canada, but foreign ownership was still limited for the time being.

It was the 1994-1995 peso and banking crisis that sparked big change. With domestic banks struggling to cope with huge levels of bad loans, Mexico decided to allow foreigners a majority stake as a way to save those flirting with collapse. The government also implemented a costly bailout plan.
Foreigners have since grabbed 12 percent of the market.
"The trend in 1997 is going to be a greater foreign presence in the market, there are going to be more very strong foreign banks," said BBV-Probursa analyst Araceli Espinosa.
The clearest example of that could be Santander, which with its Invermexico purchase got some 250 Banco Mexicano branches and is expected to add more.
The rush to set up branches by other banks has already begun. Bital had 833 branches as of September, compared with 583 in December 1995, according to government data.

Bancomer is advertising its 1,200th branch, and Banamex officials say they are opening up mini-branches in supermarkets across the country. Banamex also said it is cutting costs in order to undercut foreign rivals, though it acknowledges the foreigners bought their Mexican operations at bargain prices and have money to spare.

Even the local powerhouses have been forced to seek outside help. Bancomer, Mexico's second largest bank, sold 16 percent of its shares in March to Bank of Montreal. Serfin, the third largest bank in the system, is still seeking a partner to buy 20 percent of its capital.
Hong Kong's HSBC has been the most widely rumoured top candidate, though Serfin refuses to say which bank is in the running.

Inverlat, another big bank that has undergone government intervention, is supported by Bank of Nova Scotia, which already has a 16 percent stake and the option of expanding that to 55 percent by the year 2000.
Analysts say the process of consolidation may not be over.
"Small and medium-sized banks are going to have to link up, and you can't rule out that one or two banks will be liquidated," said Santander's Berdeja.
